subject: physics
title: Elliptical orbits and planetary data
key_idea: Planets, minor planets and comets move in elliptical orbits, with the Sun off-centre. An object moves faster when it is nearer the Sun, because gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy. The Sun's gravitational field weakens with distance, so planets further out orbit more slowly.

blocks.text: An orbit is not a perfect circle. This section covers the shape of orbits and what orbits what.

items.meaning: A stretched circle, like an oval.
A ball of ice and dust that orbits the Sun.
A smaller body that orbits the Sun, such as a dwarf planet or an asteroid.

items: Planets, minor planets and comets all have **elliptical** orbits around the Sun.
The Sun is not at the centre of the ellipse. It is off-centre.
The exception is an orbit that is approximately circular, where the Sun is at the centre.
The orbits of the planets are only slightly elliptical, so they are close to circular.

rows: Very elliptical (oval), with the Sun well off-centre

items: A comet's distance from the Sun changes a lot, so its speed changes a lot.
A planet's distance from the Sun changes little, so its speed changes little.
A planet's orbital radius and period are much greater than a moon's or satellite's.
Planets, minor planets and comets orbit the Sun in ellipses.
The Sun is off-centre, unless the orbit is almost circular.
A comet's orbit is much more elliptical than a planet's.

blocks.text: (Supplement) The speed of an object in an elliptical orbit is not constant. This section covers why.

items: An object in an elliptical orbit travels **faster** when it is closer to the Sun.
It travels **slower** when it is further from the Sun.
Energy is conserved, so the total of gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy stays constant.
Moving away from the Sun, kinetic energy transfers to gravitational potential energy, so the speed falls.
Moving towards the Sun, gravitational potential energy transfers to kinetic energy, so the speed rises.
At the closest point, potential energy is least and kinetic energy is greatest.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Statements about an object in an elliptical orbit are sorted into those true at the closest point to the Sun and those true at the furthest point.
diagram.prompt: Sort each statement into where it is true in the orbit.

items: An orbiting object is fastest when closest to the Sun.
Kinetic and gravitational potential energy are transferred to each other, and their total stays constant.

blocks.text: Gravitational field strength is the force on each kilogram of mass. This section covers what changes it.

items: At the surface of a planet, the field strength depends on the **mass** of the planet.
A planet with a larger mass has a stronger field at its surface, if the planets are similar in size.
Field strength is also different on other planets and the Moon, because their masses, sizes and densities differ.
Around a planet, the field strength **decreases** as the distance from the planet increases.
(Supplement) The same is true of the Sun: its gravitational field weakens as distance from the Sun increases.
So the orbital speeds of the planets decrease as their distance from the Sun increases.
Jupiter is further from the Sun than the Earth, so its orbital speed is lower.
The field strength falls faster than the distance rises: gravitational field strength × distance² is constant.
Doubling the distance from the centre of a planet cuts the field strength to a quarter.

items: Surface field strength depends on the mass of the planet.
Field strength decreases with distance from the planet or the Sun.
Planets further from the Sun orbit more slowly.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Questions give a table of data about planets. This section covers the patterns to look for.

items: Further from the Sun means a longer orbital period.
The larger the mass, the larger the surface gravitational field strength.
The orbital distance is an **average**, because the orbit is elliptical and the distance changes.
Planets close to the Sun generally have higher surface temperatures.
Jupiter is a large gas planet with a low density. Earth is a small rocky planet with a high density.
Jupiter has more mass than Earth because its volume is much larger, even though its density is lower.
An object falls a given height in the shortest time on the planet with the highest field strength.
In planetary data, period increases with distance from the Sun.
Mass links to surface field strength, and gas planets have low density.
Orbital distances are averages because orbits are elliptical.

checks.q: State the shape of the orbit of a comet and where the Sun is in it.
checks.a: Elliptical, with the Sun not at the centre of the ellipse.

checks.q: Explain why a comet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun.
checks.a: Gravitational potential energy transfers to kinetic energy as it moves closer. Energy is conserved, so the total stays constant and the speed increases.

checks.q: State and explain how the orbital speed of Jupiter compares with that of the Earth.
checks.a: Jupiter is slower. It is further from the Sun, where the Sun's gravitational field is weaker.

worked_example.question: Comets are balls of ice and dust. Some comets orbit the Sun. State how the speed of a comet changes as it orbits the Sun. Explain your answer using ideas about the conservation of energy.
answer_points: A comet has an elliptical orbit. Its speed is faster when it is closer to the Sun and slower when it is further away.
Energy is conserved, so energy is transferred between kinetic and gravitational energy stores and the total energy stays constant.
As the radius of the orbit decreases, gravitational energy decreases and kinetic energy increases, and the reverse when it moves away.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for the change in speed, the idea of conservation and the energy transfer.

worked_example.question: Describe how the orbit of a comet compares with the orbit of a planet.
answer_points: The comet's orbit is more elliptical (oval).
The comet's orbital path is longer.
The comet's speed varies but the planet's speed hardly changes.
The comet's orbital radius varies but the planet's does not.
The star is at the centre of the planet's orbit but not at the centre of the comet's orbit.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. Each point must compare the comet with the planet.
